Based on the healthcare Q&A matches, here's a synthesized answer to the user's question:

When primary care providers are prompted about increased patient risk due to family history, it is not clear whether this approach works. While simple prompts at the visit can improve PCPs' ability to identify high-risk patients for 6 common conditions, further studies are needed to evaluate its effectiveness.

In terms of clinical presentation, a prior preterm birth may predict an increased risk in a subsequent pregnancy. However, studies have shown that patients with a history of ACD (accelerated cervical disease) are at a higher risk of having recurrent preterm birth and cervical shortening in future pregnancies compared to women with other types of prematurity.

Regarding provider service networks, the Medicaid Demonstration in Florida appears to result in lower expenditures. However, PSNs (provider service networks) generated slightly greater reductions in expenditures compared to HMOs (health maintenance organizations). This suggests that PSNs may be a promising model for delivering care to Medicaid enrollees.

Follow-up recommendations for abnormal Papanicolaou smears can influence patient adherence, but low adherence is common. Using up to 3 reminders can improve adherence. Allocation of resources to effective methods for improving follow-up adherence may be more important than which follow-up procedure is recommended.

Regarding hypoglycaemia and cardiovascular events, severe hypoglycaemia is associated with an increased risk in people at high CV (cardiovascular) risk. However, insulin glargine-based glucose-lowering therapy appears to have a lower relative risk of CV outcomes compared to standard care. Trial registration data suggest that position emission tomography scanning can accurately change the stage or alter the treatment of almost a third of patients with advanced primary rectal cancer.

Overall, these healthcare Q&A matches indicate that prompting primary care providers about increased patient risk due to family history can have varying effects depending on the specific context and study. It is essential to evaluate the effectiveness of this approach in different scenarios and consider the limitations of the existing research findings.
